author: Nisa Patel
content:
Beyond "Mild, Medium, or Hot"

Ordering Thai food is an art that goes beyond simply choosing a heat level. Understanding how to balance dishes, share communally, and pair flavours will transform your Thai dining experience from good to extraordinary.

Understanding Heat Levels

Thai heat is measured differently than Western spice. In Thailand, dishes are typically not customised for heat — you eat them as the chef intended. However, since we're in Melbourne, we're happy to adjust:

  • Mild — gentle warmth, suitable for most palates
  • Medium> — a pleasant tingle, the way most Thai people eat at home
  • Hot — authentic Thai heat, not for the faint-hearted. Expect to sweat, but also to feel alive

Building the Perfect Thai Meal

Thai meals are designed to be shared, not eaten as single courses. Here's how to build a balanced meal for two:

  1. One starter to share — something light like Chicken Satay or Crispy Spring Rolls
  2. One soup — Tom Yum Goong or Tom Kha Gai to warm the palate
  3. One curry — Green Curry or Panang for the rich, coconut-creamy element
  4. One stir-fry or noodle dish — Pad Thai or Holy Basil Stir-fry for contrast
  5. One salad — Som Tam for a refreshing, acidic counterpoint
  6. Jasmine rice — the foundation that ties everything together
  7. Dessert — Mango Sticky Rice to end on a sweet note

The Sharing Philosophy

In Thailand, food is communal. Everyone gets a plate of rice, and all dishes are placed in the centre of the table. You take a little of everything, creating your own perfect bite each time. This approach ensures variety and balance in every mouthful.

Don't Skip the Condiments

Every good Thai table has four condiments: fish sauce with chili, dried chili flakes, sugar, and vinegar. These aren't just for show — Thais use them to customise each dish as they eat. A dash of fish sauce adds saltiness, a pinch of sugar balances sourness, and chili flakes add heat where needed.

author: Chef Somchai
content:
The Flavour Philosophy of Tom Yum

Tom Yum Goong perfectly embodies the Thai culinary philosophy of balancing contrasting flavours. The name itself tells the story: tom means boiled, yum refers to the spicy-sour salad-like quality, and goong means prawn. Together, they create something far greater than the sum of its parts.

The Holy Trinity of Thai Aromatics

Three ingredients form the aromatic backbone of Tom Yum:

  • Lemongrass — citrusy, fresh, and slightly sweet
  • Galangal — a cousin of ginger with piney, peppery notes
  • Kaffir lime leaves — intensely fragrant with a unique citrus perfume

These three are bruised and simmered to release their essential oils, creating a fragrant broth that perfumes the entire restaurant when a fresh pot is made.

Clear vs. Creamy

There are two styles of Tom Yum. Tom Yum Nam Sai (clear broth) is light, sharp, and intensely flavoured. Tom Yum Nam Khon (creamy) adds evaporated milk or coconut cream for a richer, smoother texture. At Vermont Thai, we serve the clear style — letting the natural flavours of tiger prawns and aromatics shine through.

Our Tom Yum Goong

We use only tiger prawns in our Tom Yum Goong, simmered in a fiery, tangy broth infused with fresh lemongrass, galangal, kaffir lime leaves, and bird's eye chili. Served with fluffy jasmine rice, it's the kind of dish that warms you from the inside out and leaves you craving more.

At $26, it's one of our most popular soups — and for good reason. Come taste why Tom Yum Goong is considered one of the world's greatest soups.

author: Chef Somchai
content:
When Simplicity is Perfection

Of all Thailand's desserts, Mango Sticky Rice (Khao Niao Mamuang) is perhaps the most beloved. It requires only three main ingredients — glutinous rice, fresh mango, and coconut cream — yet when prepared correctly, it's one of the most satisfying desserts in the world.

The Rice

The secret lies in the rice. Glutinous rice (also called sticky rice or sweet rice) must be soaked for at least 4 hours, then steamed — not boiled — in a traditional bamboo steamer or cheesecloth-lined pot. The steaming process gives the rice its characteristically chewy, tender texture while keeping each grain intact.

The Coconut Sauce

While the rice steams, a warm coconut sauce is prepared by gently heating coconut cream with sugar and a pinch of salt. This sauce is folded into the hot rice, giving it a glossy, fragrant sweetness. Extra sauce is drizzled on top just before serving.

The Mango

Only the best mangoes will do. In Thailand, that means Nam Dok Mai — an elongated, golden-yellow variety with impossibly sweet, buttery flesh. In Melbourne, we source the closest equivalent and ensure every mango is perfectly ripe before serving.

Our Mango Sticky Rice

At Vermont Thai, our Mango Sticky Rice is made fresh throughout the day. Sweet glutinous rice is steamed with coconut cream, served alongside fresh ripe mango, and drizzled with warm coconut sauce. At $14, it's the perfect ending to any Thai meal.

Seasonal Special

Mango Sticky Rice tastes best during mango season (November to March in Thailand). We celebrate this with special presentations and pairing suggestions — ask our staff about seasonal dessert specials.

author: Nisa Patel
content:
Born in Thailand's Northeast

Som Tam (also spelled Som Tum) originates from Isaan, Thailand's northeastern region that shares cultural and culinary ties with Laos. In Isaan, Som Tam isn't just food — it's a daily ritual, a social connector, and a point of fierce regional pride.

The Mortar and Pestle Technique

Traditional Som Tam is made by pounding ingredients in a large clay mortar (khrok) with a wooden pestle. This gentle bruising releases flavours without destroying the texture — a technique that's nearly impossible to replicate with a food processor.

The classic ingredients include shredded green papaya, long beans, cherry tomatoes, dried shrimp, peanuts, garlic, bird's eye chili, lime juice, fish sauce, and palm sugar. Each ingredient is added in sequence and lightly pounded.

Many Styles, One Salad

There are dozens of Som Tam variations across Thailand:

  • Som Tam Thai — the sweet, mild version with dried shrimp and peanuts (most common)
  • Som Tam Lao — the original Isaan style, saltier and funkier with fermented fish sauce (padaek)
  • Som Tam Pu — with whole salted crabs for extra umami
  • Som Tam Pla Ra — with fermented fish paste, the most pungent version

How to Eat It

In Thailand, Som Tam is always eaten with sticky rice (khao niao). You pinch a ball of sticky rice, dip it into the salad juices, and eat it together. It's traditionally served with grilled chicken (gai yang) and raw vegetables. At Vermont Thai, we serve it alongside our menu so you can create your own perfect combination.

Our Som Tam

Our Som Tam is pounded fresh to order with lime, chili, fish sauce, palm sugar, peanuts, and dried shrimp. It's one of our most popular dishes — bold, refreshing, and authentically spicy. Not for the faint of heart, but absolutely unforgettable.

author: Nisa Patel
content:
The Heartbeat of Thai Cuisine

Street food isn't just cheap eating in Thailand — it's the heartbeat of the culture. Walk through any Thai city at dusk and you'll find sizzling woks, charcoal grills, and the intoxicating aroma of garlic, chili, and fresh herbs filling the air. It's where the best food is often found.

Iconic Street Food Dishes

Some of the world's most beloved Thai dishes started as street food:

  • Pad Thai — originally sold from pushcarts during Thailand's nation-building era
  • Som Tam — green papaya salad pounded fresh to order in mortar and pestle
  • Moo Ping — grilled pork skewers marinated in coconut milk and palm sugar
  • Kanom Krok — sweet coconut pancakes cooked in cast-iron pans
  • Gai Yang — charcoal-grilled marinated chicken, smoky and caramelised

The Night Market Experience

Thai night markets (talat yen) are sensory overload in the best possible way. Neon lights, sizzling sounds, friendly vendors calling out specials, and an endless parade of dishes you've never tried before. The atmosphere is as important as the food itself.

Bringing Street Food to Melbourne

At Vermont Thai, we bring the spirit of Thai street food to Melbourne. Dishes like our Moo Ping (grilled pork skewers with sticky rice), Som Tam (green papaya salad), and Kanom Krok (coconut pancakes) are directly inspired by the street vendors of Bangkok and Chiang Mai. We believe you shouldn't have to fly 8 hours for authentic Thai flavours.

Tips for Your First Street Food Experience

If you're visiting Thailand, eat where the locals eat. Long queues at a humble cart usually mean exceptional food. Don't be afraid of spice — but always ask for "mai phet" (not spicy) if you're unsure. And carry small bills; most vendors don't accept cards.

author: Chef Somchai
content:
More Than Just "Spicy Soup"

Thai curries are worlds apart from Indian or Japanese curries. They're built on a foundation of fresh curry paste (not dried powder), coconut milk, and an intricate balance of herbs, spices, and aromatics. Every curry tells a story of Thailand's regional diversity.

Green Curry (Kaeng Khiao Wan)

The most vibrant of all Thai curries, green curry gets its colour from fresh green chilies, cilantro roots, and Thai basil. Despite its fiery appearance, it's actually one of the milder curries when prepared traditionally. Our Green Curry Chicken features tender chicken simmered in fresh green curry paste with coconut milk, Thai eggplant, bamboo shoots, and sweet basil leaves.

Red Curry (Kaeng Phet)

Red curry uses dried red chilies, giving it a deeper, earthier heat compared to green. It's versatile and pairs beautifully with duck — our Red Curry Duck combines pan-seared duck with coconut milk, cherry tomatoes, pineapple, and Thai basil for a harmonious balance of sweet and savoury.

Panang Curry

Thicker and more concentrated than other curries, Panang has a velvety texture with pronounced peanut and kaffir lime notes. Our Panang Curry with sliced chicken is rich, aromatic, and deeply satisfying — perfect for those who love intense flavour without overwhelming heat.

Massaman Curry

Influenced by Persian and Indian cuisine, Massaman is the mildest and most complex Thai curry. Warm spices like cardamom, cinnamon, and cloves blend with coconut milk and peanuts. Our Massaman Beef features slow-braised beef that falls apart after hours of gentle simmering.

Which Curry Should You Try?

If you're new to Thai curry, start with Massaman for its gentle warmth. If you love bold, herbaceous flavours, go for Green Curry. For something rich and nutty, Panang is your answer. And if you want a classic with depth, Red Curry Duck never disappoints.

author: Chef Somchai
content:
A Curry with a Global History

Massaman curry is unlike any other Thai curry. Its story begins in the 17th century, when Persian merchants and diplomats brought their spice traditions to the court of Ayutthaya, the capital of Siam (now Thailand). The result was a curry that bridges Middle Eastern and Southeast Asian cuisines — a true fusion dish centuries before fusion became a trend.

The Spice Profile

What sets Massaman apart is its warm spice blend:

  • Cardamom — floral and eucalyptus-like
  • Cinnamon — warm and sweet
  • Cloves — intense and aromatic
  • Star anise — licorice-like sweetness
  • Nutmeg — earthy and warming

These spices are ground into a paste with dried red chilies, lemongrass, galangal, garlic, shallots, and shrimp paste — then simmered in coconut milk with potatoes, onions, roasted peanuts, and beef.

The Slow-Braise Secret

Great Massaman requires patience. The beef must be slow-braised for hours until it's fork-tender and the connective tissue has melted into the sauce, creating a rich, glossy gravy. At Vermont Thai, our Massaman Beef simmers for a minimum of 4 hours, developing layers of flavour that can't be rushed.

Our Massaman Beef

At $27, our Massaman Beef is one of our most popular curries — and one of CNN Travel's "World's 50 Most Delicious Foods." We serve it with fluffy jasmine rice, and we recommend pairing it with a cold Thai Iced Tea or a refreshing Coconut Water to balance the richness.

A Curry for Everyone

Massaman is the most approachable Thai curry for newcomers. Its mild heat, complex spices, and comforting richness make it universally appealing. If you've never tried Thai curry, start here — it might just change your life.

author: Chef Somchai
content:
A Dish Born from Nation-Building

Pad Thai wasn't always Thailand's national dish. In the 1930s, Prime Minister Plaek Phibunsongkhram launched a campaign to modernise Thailand and create a unified national identity. Part of this effort was promoting a single "national dish" — and Pad Thai was chosen. The government distributed recipes, set up street carts, and encouraged citizens to eat noodles as a symbol of Thai-ness.

The Perfect Balance of Flavours

What makes Pad Thai extraordinary is its balance of the four fundamental Thai tastes: sweet from palm sugar, sour from tamarind, salty from fish sauce, and a hint of spice from dried chili. At Vermont Thai, we honour this balance by making our tamarind sauce fresh daily and using only premium rice noodles that absorb flavour without turning mushy.

Our Pad Thai Prawns

Our Pad Thai Prawns features wok-tossed rice noodles with tiger prawns, egg, bean sprouts, and crushed peanuts in house-made tamarind sauce. The key is high heat — our woks burn at over 300°C, creating that sought-after wok hei (breath of the wok) that gives the noodles a subtle smokiness you can't replicate at home.

Tips for the Best Pad Thai Experience

  • Squeeze fresh lime over the noodles just before eating — it brightens every flavour
  • Mix the crushed peanuts through the noodles for extra crunch
  • Add a dash of chili flakes if you prefer more heat
  • Pair it with a cold Thai iced tea to balance the savoury richness

Next time you visit Vermont Thai, try our Pad Thai Prawns and taste the difference that tradition and technique make.

author: Nisa Patel
content:
More Than Just Iced Tea

Thai Iced Tea (Cha Yen) is nothing like the iced tea you find elsewhere. Its distinctive orange colour, creamy sweetness, and complex spice notes make it one of the most recognisable Thai beverages in the world. It's the perfect companion to spicy Thai food, and many would argue a meal isn't complete without it.

The Ingredients

Traditional Cha Yen starts with strongly brewed Ceylon tea (or a Thai tea mix called cha dam). The tea is simmered with star anise, tamarind seed, and sometimes vanilla or cardamom. While still hot, sweetened condensed milk is added, creating a rich, creamy base. It's then poured over ice and often topped with evaporated milk for a beautiful layered effect.

The Orange Colour

The vibrant orange hue of Thai iced tea comes from food colouring added to the tea mix. In Thailand, most tea vendors use a mix of red and yellow food dyes. While it might seem unusual, the colour has become an integral part of the Cha Yen experience.

Hot vs. Cold

While Cha Yen (iced) is the most famous version, Cha Ron (hot Thai tea) is equally delicious and perfect for Melbourne's cooler months. Same ingredients, same preparation — just served steaming hot.

Our Thai Iced Tea

At Vermont Thai, our Thai Iced Tea is made with strongly brewed Ceylon tea, star anise, and sweetened condensed milk, served over ice with its signature vibrant orange hue. At just $7.50, it's the perfect way to cool down after a fiery Tom Yum or a spicy Som Tam.

Fun Pairings

Try Thai Iced Tea with:

  • Massaman Beef — the creamy tea balances the warm curry spices
  • Mango Sticky Rice — doubles down on coconut sweetness for dessert lovers
  • Pad Thai — the classic pairing, sweet tea meets tangy noodles

author: Nisa Patel
content:
Building Your Thai Pantry

Thai cuisine relies on a handful of key ingredients that appear across countless dishes. With these five essentials, you can start cooking authentic Thai food at home — no shortcuts needed.

1. Fish Sauce (Nam Pla)

Fish sauce is the salt of Southeast Asian cooking. Made from fermented anchovies, it adds umami depth that table salt simply cannot replicate. A good quality fish sauce (like Three Crabs or Tra Chang) should be salty, complex, and slightly sweet — never purely fishy.

2. Coconut Milk

Not to be confused with coconut water, coconut milk is made by blending grated coconut meat with water and pressing the liquid. It forms the creamy base of most Thai curries and soups. Always buy full-fat coconut milk (not "lite") for authentic results.

3. Palm Sugar

Thai palm sugar has a caramel-like richness that regular white sugar lacks. It balances the heat and sourness in Thai dishes beautifully. Look for it in block form at Asian grocers — you can grate it or shave it as needed.

4. Lemongrass

Fresh lemongrass is irreplaceable in Thai cooking. Its citrusy, floral aroma forms the backbone of soups like Tom Yum and Tom Kha. Bruise the stalks with the back of a knife before adding them to release maximum flavour.

5. Thai Bird's Eye Chili (Prik Kee Noo)

These tiny chilies pack serious heat. They're used fresh in salads, stir-fries, and dipping sauces. Start with half a chili if you're heat-sensitive — you can always add more. For the freshest flavour, slice them just before cooking.

Bonus: Kaffir Lime Leaves & Galangal

If you can find them, kaffir lime leaves and galangal (Thai ginger) will elevate your Thai cooking dramatically. They're the secret ingredients that give Thai food its distinctive aroma.

Visit your local Asian grocer in Melbourne — Victoria Market and Springvale have excellent selections of all these ingredients.

author: Vermont Thai Team
content:
Where It All Began

Vermont Thai was born from a simple dream: to bring the authentic flavours of Thailand to Melbourne without compromise. Our head chef, trained in Bangkok's finest kitchens and Thailand's legendary street food scene, envisioned a restaurant where every dish tells a story of tradition, technique, and passion.

The Bangkok Years

Before Vermont Thai, our chef spent over a decade honing their craft in Bangkok — from the humble street stalls of Yaowarat (Chinatown) to upscale restaurants along Sukhumvit Road. These experiences shaped a cooking philosophy that values authenticity above all else.

Every recipe on our menu has been tested, refined, and perfected. Some have been passed down through generations, while others are creative interpretations that honour traditional techniques while embracing local Australian ingredients.

Finding Our Home in Melbourne

Melbourne was a natural choice. The city's multicultural food scene, appreciation for quality ingredients, and adventurous diners make it the perfect home for authentic Thai cuisine. We wanted to be more than just another Thai restaurant — we wanted to be a bridge between two food-loving cultures.

Our Philosophy

At Vermont Thai, we believe in three principles:

  1. Authenticity — every dish must taste like it would in Thailand
  2. Freshness — we make our curry pastes, sauces, and stocks from scratch daily
  3. Hospitality — Thai culture values warm, generous service, and we carry that spirit into everything we do

Looking Forward

As we grow, our commitment to authenticity remains unwavering. We continue to source the best Thai ingredients, refine our techniques, and explore new dishes from Thailand's diverse regional cuisines. Whether it's a classic Pad Thai or a lesser-known Northern Thai specialty, every plate that leaves our kitchen carries the soul of Thailand.

Thank you for being part of our journey. Sawasdee khrap!

author: Chef Somchai
content:
A Taste of the North

Khao Soi hails from Northern Thailand (Lanna region), where the cuisine is distinct from the central Thai food most foreigners know. Influenced by Burmese and Chinese cooking, Khao Soi features egg noodles in a rich coconut curry broth — topped with crispy fried noodles that add an irresistible crunch.

The Two-Texture Magic

What makes Khao Soi special is the interplay of textures. You get soft, boiled egg noodles swimming in the curry, contrasted with a generous handful of crispy fried noodles scattered on top. As you eat, the crispy noodles soften slightly in the broth, creating a constantly evolving mouthfeel.

The Broth

Traditional Khao Soi broth is made from a paste of dried red chilies, turmeric, galangal, lemongrass, garlic, shallots, and shrimp paste, simmered in coconut milk with a splash of chicken or pork stock. The result is a deeply aromatic, slightly sweet, and mildly spicy curry that's unlike any other Thai soup.

Our Khao Soi at Vermont Thai

Our Khao Soi features tender chicken in a house-made coconut curry broth with egg noodles, pickled mustard greens, and crispy noodle topping. We add a side of fresh shallots, lime wedge, and chili paste so you can customise each bowl to your taste.

At $24.50, it's a journey to the streets of Chiang Mai in every spoonful. If you haven't tried Khao Soi yet, it might just become your new favourite Thai dish.

Serving Suggestions

Pair Khao Soi with our Thai Iced Tea for the classic Northern Thai combination. The sweet, creamy tea perfectly balances the rich, spicy broth.
